pageDescription: Foundations, information processing, and optical quantum networks

overview.title: Research overview
paragraphs: My research seeks to understand what is genuinely nonclassical about quantum theory and to translate that understanding into useful protocols for quantum information processing. My work combines quantum foundations and quantum information theory with experimental and theoretical photonic quantum information processing.
My current research is organized around three themes:
topics: developing operational frameworks for defining, certifying, and quantifying quantum nonclassicality;
advancing optical quantum information processing for communication, sensing, and quantum networks;
exploring broader directions in quantum information and AI-assisted quantum science.

themes.title: Foundations of Quantum Nonclassicality
paragraphs: A central question in my research is how to identify what is genuinely nonclassical about quantum theory. Rather than relying on a particular mathematical representation,  I'd like to approach this question operationally; I seek definitions and tests of nonclassicality that can be expressed directly in terms of laboratory procedures and experimental statistics.

My work studies several related manifestations of nonclassicality, including measurement incompatibility, generalized contextuality, entanglement, quantum steering, Bell nonlocality, and negativity in quasiprobability representations. I am particularly interested in understanding the relationships among these phenomena and in developing systematic methods to **define**, **certify**, and **quantify** the resources they represent.

From a foundational perspective, this program aims to distinguish genuinely quantum phenomena from effects that can arise through classical mechanisms, such as incomplete information, epistemic restrictions, or limited operational access. Comparisons with broader post-quantum theories can also help reveal which features of nonclassicality are specific to quantum theory, which extend beyond it, and which structural principles constrain the correlations permitted by nature.

These questions are also important for quantum technology. Identifying the relevant nonclassical resource can explain the origin of a quantum advantage in an existing protocol. It can also suggest new measurements, encodings, and information-processing tasks that use the resource more effectively.

subthemes.title: Leibnizian nonclassicality through generalized noncontextuality

figuresBefore.alt: Operational diagram asking whether an individual quantum process admits a classical ontological representation.
figuresBefore.caption: Classical explainability of an individual quantum process.

paragraphs: I use generalized noncontextuality to formulate a Leibnizian notion of classical explainability: operationally indistinguishable procedures should be represented identically in a classical model. This principle provides a unified way to define the classical–nonclassical boundary for individual quantum processes and to develop practical methods for certifying and quantifying nonclassicality.

subthemes.title: Measurement incompatibility, quantum steering, and Bell nonlocality
paragraphs: I study the close operational relationships among measurement incompatibility, quantum steering, and Bell nonlocality. My work asks when general measurements reveal steering, how sharply the boundary between steerable and unsteerable correlations can be characterized, and what classical resources are required to simulate steering experiments. I also investigate activation phenomena, in which quantum channels that individually cannot distribute CHSH nonlocality can do so when used together.

papers.note: An exact criterion for when unital qubit channels make every POVM jointly measurable, with corresponding steering boundaries for two-qubit states.

papers.note: The shared-randomness resources required to simulate entangled states in steering experiments.

papers.title: Channel Activation of CHSH Nonlocality
papers.note: How channels that individually destroy CHSH nonlocality can activate nonlocal state distribution when used together.

subthemes.title: Quantum protocols through the lens of foundational concepts
paragraphs: Foundational concepts can clarify where a quantum advantage comes from and how to use it more effectively. I apply this perspective to communication protocols enabled by single-particle superposition and to entanglement-assisted sensing under superselection-rule constraints, where identifying the relevant physical restriction leads directly to sharper performance limits and improved protocols.

papers.title: Building Multiple Access Channels with a Single Particle
papers.note: How single-particle superposition enables communication strategies unavailable to a classical particle.

papers.title: Criteria for Optimal Entanglement-Assisted Long Baseline Telescopy
papers.note: A superselection-rule framework for identifying optimal entanglement resources and precision limits in quantum telescopy.

themes.title: Optical Quantum Information Processing and Quantum Networks
paragraphs: My background spans both theory and experiment in optical quantum information. This training has given me a practical understanding of both the capabilities and the limitations of photonic quantum technologies.

Photonic platforms face significant challenges as architectures for scalable, universal quantum computation, particularly when compared with leading solid-state platforms. However, photons are exceptionally well suited to transmitting quantum information and connecting distant systems. Optical quantum information processing therefore plays a central role in quantum communication, distributed quantum sensing, and metrology.

subthemes.title: Quantum-enhanced sensing and astronomical imaging
paragraphs: I develop and analyze protocols for imaging astronomical objects using quantum communication, shared entanglement, and nonstandard optical measurements. This includes establishing fundamental precision limits, designing protocols that approach those limits, and investigating experimentally realizable measurements for sub-Rayleigh imaging, including our array-SPADE approach.

subthemes.title: Quantum communication and resource distribution
paragraphs: I study how quantum information and nonclassical resources can be transmitted, certified, and used across noisy and experimentally realistic networks. My interests include frequency-bin encodings used in multimode free-space channels, entanglement distribution, and communication protocols based on limited quantum resources.

papers.note: Communication rates and quantum advantages in multiple-access channels constructed from a single particle.

papers.title: Channel Activation of CHSH Nonlocality
papers.note: How network structure can activate nonlocal resources that are inaccessible through individual noisy channels.

subthemes.title: Real-world quantum-network testbeds
paragraphs: I have also helped lead the development of realistic quantum-network links that serve as testbeds for quantum networking in practice. This work connects photon-source engineering, fiber transmission, entanglement distribution, control systems, and public-facing quantum-science infrastructure.

papers.note: Experimental engineering and characterization of photonic quantum sources.

papers.title: Fiber-Based Photon-Pair Generation
papers.note: A tutorial treatment of spontaneous four-wave mixing and photon-pair engineering in optical fibers.

themes.title: Broader Directions in Quantum Information and AI for Quantum Science
paragraphs: I am broadly interested in other areas of quantum information science, particularly quantum Shannon theory, quantum error correction, quantum learning theory, and the principles governing information processing across different physical platforms. I would like to deepen my understanding of experimental architectures beyond optics and investigate which ideas and resources can be transferred between platforms.

I am also interested in the emerging role of artificial intelligence in quantum science. AI has become a useful collaborator for literature synthesis, analytic and numerical exploration, hypothesis generation, and the discovery of unexpected connections between different areas of physics. At the same time, frontier problems in quantum science provide demanding tests of whether an AI can perform sustained scientific reasoning rather than reproduce familiar patterns.

My work on [CritPt: A Frontier Physics Research Benchmark](https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.26574) contributes to evaluating AI reasoning on research-level physics problems. Looking forward, I am interested in developing AI-assisted approaches that strengthen physical understanding, help researchers explore difficult problems, and support—rather than obscure—the conceptual reasoning at the heart of quantum science.
